An open format for AI conversations — spec v1 · curt-format@1.2.0 · MIT

A .curt file is UTF-8 JSON — the whole thread in one
file. Images and tool calls ride verbatim, unknown fields survive
foreign readers, and a corrupted file is rejected whole, never
half-imported. Born in Curtis AI Chat, owned by no one.

2026-10-14 design-review 001.curt

.CURT — THE FILE, OPENED

WHAT EVERY CONFORMING READER OWES YOU

magic"curtis-conversation" — exact

version1, the number — a string "1" is a rejection

fidelitybase64 images and tool calls ride in content, verbatim

toleranceone leading UTF-8 BOM ignored; writers never emit it

round-tripunknown fields preserved on re-save ✓

licenseMIT — spec, reference code, schema, fixtures

OPEN · MIT

- conformance27 vectors · passing in CI

- audit2026-10-14 · addendum 11-01 · public

- implementations11 — read, write, or both

A .curt file is UTF-8 JSON, tab-indented by convention.
The generator field lets a writer sign its work —
readers must ignore it: presence, absence, or value never affects
parsing. Declared capabilities ride in extensions.

Fig. 1 — the envelope, annotated

{
"curt": "curtis-conversation",
"version": 1,
"generator": "your-app@1.2.3",
"extensions": ["images-inline", "usage-metadata"],
"conversation": {
"id": "conv_001",
"title": "Thursday's thread",
"createdAt": 1760000000000,
"updatedAt": 1760000600000,
"messages": [
{ "id": "m1", "role": "user",
"content": "hello", "timestamp": 1760000000000 },
{ "id": "m2", "role": "assistant",
"content": "hi back", "model": "…",
"timestamp": 1760000001000 }
]
}
}

The envelope, field by field:

fieldrequiredmeaning

curtyesmagic — must be exactly "curtis-conversation"

versionyesformat version; this spec is 1

generatornoprovenance, "writer-name@version" — readers must ignore

extensionsnonames from the registry — never a validation input

conversationyesid, title, createdAt, updatedAt, messages

roleyesuser · assistant · system · tool

modelnoprovider model id, typically on assistant messages

the spec
and rendered in the
docs;
a non-normative
JSON Schema
ships for tooling. The reference implementation is TypeScript, zero
dependencies:

import { serializeCurt, parseCurt, curtFilename } from 'curt-format';

const body = serializeCurt(conversation, 'my-app@1.0.0');
const back = parseCurt(body); // CurtConversation | null — null means invalid
const name = curtFilename(back!); // 2025-10-09 my-thread 001.curt

A READER ACCEPTS A FILE WHEN, AND ONLY WHEN

- 01

The body parses as JSON — after ignoring at most one leading UTF-8 BOM, because Windows editors prepend one anyway.

- 02

curt is exactly "curtis-conversation" and version is exactly the number 1.

- 03

The conversation carries id and title as strings, timestamps as numbers, and a messages array in which every entry passes message validation.

Anything else is a rejection — whole-file, not a best-effort parse.
Many conversations travel as a zip of .curt files.
Version 1 never changes meaning; later revisions only clarify, so
version-1 files stay readable forever.

Writers declare named capabilities in a top-level
extensions array. A reader that doesn't know one
ignores it and never rejects over it. An entry moves
draft → stable when two independent
implementations round-trip it. The registry is additive by rule:
new entries never change how existing v1 files parse.

namestatuspurposeemitted by

images-inlinestableimage payloads ride inside contentplugin · porter · web · cloud · ai-tech

usage-metadatastableper-message tokens, cost, providerporter · web · ai-tech

tool-linkagedrafttool calls linked to their resultsporter · ai-tech · curt-convert

agent-contextdraftagent and swarm provenanceplugin · porter · cloud · ai-tech

consensus-receiptdraftsigned k-of-n consensus bound to the transcript evidencetractum

Full field definitions per entry:
EXTENSIONS.md,
with per-entry pages in the
extension registry docs.

Implementations run executable vectors from
conformance/
and claim the levels they pass — self-reported, but reproducible
from the vectors. The reference implementation runs them in CI and
passes L1–L4. The ladder is explained in the
conformance docs.

- L1 · CORE
must
Magic and version exact-match, whole-file rejection, one leading BOM tolerated, unknown fields preserved on round-trip, any JSON-number timestamp accepted.

- L2 · NAMED
should
curtFilename implements the <date> <slug> <suffix>.curt algorithm exactly.

- L3 · BULK
may
The zip-of-.curt convention: entry names from curtFilename, readers never depend on names, corrupted entries reported rather than silently dropped.

- L4+ · EXTENSION
may
Per-extension vectors — an extension's presence or malformation never causes rejection.

Ecosystem status — who is in, who passes what, where conformance
has drifted — is tracked in
CAPABILITIES.md,
audited 2026-10-14.

consumerroler · wcarries

curtis pluginimport · export · backupR + Wvendored copy

curt-openwithoffline viewer — double-click any .curtRhand-rolled port

porterconverter + verify oracleR + Wvendored oracle

curtis-webexport endpointWhand-rolled

curtis-cloudshared libraryR + Wvendored mirror

curtis-ai-techembedded converter + docsR + Winline copy

tractumsigned consensus receiptsR + Wown validator

curt-vcon.curt ⇄ vCon bridgeR + Wnpm curt-format

curt-convertClaude Code JSONL → .curtWnpm curt-format

curt-openwebuiOpen WebUI exporter (local)Wnpm curt-format

Every implementation here is the author's own — the first outside
consumer is still the open item. The three newest
(curt-vcon,
curt-convert,
curt-openwebui)
depend on the
curt-format package directly; the five original
application readers still vendor or hand-roll the rules, so a
spec revision lands in five places by hand. The ladder from ten
copies to one dependency is written down in the audit.

Why a conversation format needs to exist at all — the export trap,
the portability right that fails without interoperable formats,
the landscape of vendor exports, training formats, transport
protocols, and containers — is written up as a preprint.

.curt: A Conversations-First, LLM-Native File Format with
Executable Conformance for AI Chat Portability.
Jordan Newell, 2026.
preprint · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23864677

Full text lives in
the preprint.
Citability: the DOI is live —
10.5281/zenodo.23864677
(CC-BY); arXiv (cs.CY) pending an endorsement, and the paper mirrors
there when it lands. The claim, cross-checked against the 2025–26 literature:
scholarship reached generative AI — model internals, generated
data, agentic portability — but never the conversation archive,
and the one open export spec stops at a generic transcript. The
slot is open. The paper is the argument; this format, with its
executable conformance vectors, is the answer.

## Adopt — make your app speak .curt
Source: https://dotcurt.org/adopt/

.curt

the format
post

Adopt the format — curt-format@1.2.0 · MIT · 27 vectors in CI

The format is free — the move is yours. One afternoon of work buys your
users a conversation file that never loses anything and never goes stale.

Conformance vectors
curt-format on npm

$
npm install curt-format
copy

curt-format@1.2.0 — package manifest

WHAT SHIPS IN THE BOX

ZERO DEPENDENCIES · TYPESCRIPT · MIT

serializeCurtconversation + your generator id → file body

parseCurtbody → conversation, or null — whole-file, never half

curtFilename<date> <slug> <suffix>.curt, from immutable fields

guardsisCurtMessage · isCurtConversation, the spec's predicates

schemacurt-v1.schema.json rides along ✓

MIT · V1

- 01
Full fidelity — base64 images and tool calls ride in content, verbatim. No flattening, no &ldquo;best effort&rdquo;.

- 02
Unknown fields survive a re-save. Your app's extras aren't a liability.

- 03
One diffable UTF-8 file per conversation. Archives, version control, and grep all just work.

- 04
MIT across the board — spec, reference code, schema, fixtures. (Curtis applications themselves are BUSL; the format never is.)

For app developers

The library handles the envelope, the BOM, and the unknown fields.
What's left is your integration — and the proof that it holds.

import { serializeCurt, parseCurt, curtFilename } from 'curt-format';

const body = serializeCurt(conversation, 'my-app@1.0.0');
const back = parseCurt(body); // CurtConversation | null — null means invalid
const file = curtFilename(back!); // 2026-10-14 design-review 001.curt

Also in the box: isCurtMessage and isCurtConversation —
the spec's validation predicates as type guards — plus the envelope
constants CURT_MAGIC and CURT_VERSION.
Round-trip a real conversation and confirm unknown fields survive;
that is the whole L1 bar.

How to claim conformance

- 01

Run the executable vectors. Everything is plain JSON in
conformance/vectors/:
core.json (L1, 13 cases), named.json (L2, 7),
bulk.json (L3, rules and a canonical example),
extensions.json (L4, 6). Twenty-seven checks in all —
if your parser accepts what they accept and rejects what they reject,
you match the level.

- 02

Update your row in capabilities.json.
Set conformanceLevel (e.g. "L1", "L1+L2"),
the extensions you emit and accept, and lastAudited.
Open a PR — CAPABILITIES.md
carries the human-readable audit.

- 03

Link a reproducible run. A CI job or script in your repo
that executes the vectors. Claims are self-reported — and reproducible
by anyone from the same files.

levelobligationthe bar

L1 · coremustmagic and version exact-match, one leading BOM tolerated, whole-file rejection, unknown fields preserved on round-trip

L2 · namedshouldcurtFilename implements <date> <slug> <suffix>.curt exactly

L3 · bulkmayzip of .curt files; corrupted entries reported, never silently dropped

L4+ · extensionmayper-extension vectors; presence or malformation never causes rejection

Level definitions and vector formats:
conformance/README.md.
The reference implementation runs all twenty-seven in CI and passes L1–L4.

For end users

In production across six apps — five audited 2026-10-14, the sixth
(curt-openwith) added 2026-11-01 — all the author's own,
stated plainly. If you use any of them, your conversations are
already files — one per thread, portable between them all.

appwhat it does with .curt

curtis pluginObsidian — import, export, full-backup zip

curt-openwithdouble-click any .curt file — offline viewer (Windows + macOS + Linux)

porterconverter (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini → .curt and back) + verify oracle

curtis-webchat app — export single .curt and bulk zip

curtis-cloudshared library — import/export serialization

curtis-ai-techdocs + embedded converter with inline preview

The tracker carries eleven entries — the newest are tractum, a Python
SDK that emits signed consensus receipts, and the npm-era bridges and
converters built on curt-format. The honest score: eleven
entries, one author; four depend on
curt-format directly (curt-vcon, curt-convert,
curt-wildchat, curt-openwebui — the first three on npm since
2026-11-01), while the five original applications still vendor or
hand-roll the rules. First outside
consumer sets the tone;
the launch post doesn't
pretend otherwise.

For tool builders

- 01
JSON Schema. Non-normative, for tooling — ships inside the npm package at curt-format/schema/curt-v1.schema.json. Editors, linters, and validators in any language.

- 02
Round-trip fixtures. tests/fixtures/ — basic.curt, empty.curt, rich.curt, roles.curt — the same files the reference tests run against. Seed your own suite with them.

- 03
Extension registry. New capability is a PR to EXTENSIONS.md: name, status, the exact fields, any vectors. An entry moves draft → stable when two independent implementations round-trip it.

The registry today:

extensionstatuswhat it carries

images-inlinestablebase64 images in content, verbatim

usage-metadatastabletokens / cost / provider per message

tool-linkagedrafttool calls linked to their results

agent-contextdraftagent/system context alongside the thread

consensus-receiptdraftsigned consensus decisions (tractum, sole impl)

Draft → stable requires two independent implementations round-tripping it. consensus-receipt needs one more.

- 01
Will the spec change under me? No. Core is frozen at v1; evolution is registry-only, and registry entries never change how existing files parse.

- 02
Who decides? One maintainer, BDFL — deliberately. A format with six committees has no direction.

- 03
What does draft mean for me? Emit it if you want. Readers must ignore unknown extensions and never reject over them, so nothing breaks.

- 04
License? MIT — spec, reference code, schema, fixtures. Build a business on it if you like.

NOT YET — STATED PLAINLY

dot_curt are welcome.

curt-format yet — five vendored
copies and one hand-rolled. Yours can be the first real dependency;
the tracker has a row waiting.

Convert in the browser — nothing leaves this tab

Drag a ChatGPT or Claude export onto this page and it files every conversation as a dot curt file — converted, named, previewed, and zipped entirely in your browser. There is no server to upload to; the whole porter is this page.

Drop an export here, or click to choose

conversations.json · claude json · export zip · curt

Several files at once are fine, zips included. ChatGPT conversations are read by walking the mapping tree from its current node, so a regenerated answer stays in its branch and out of your file. Claude exports are read from their chat message lists. Bare .curt files are validated whole: a corrupted file is reported, never half-imported. Files are written by porter-web@0.1.0 through the reference implementation, vendored into this page.

Paste the contents of a ChatGPT conversations.json or a Claude export — the same conversion runs on the paste, and nothing is uploaded anywhere. A single .curt body pasted as JSON works too.

## Curt Conversation Exporter — the browser extension
Source: https://dotcurt.org/extension/

.curt

the format
post
listen
try
viewer
paper
conformance
github

Curt Conversation Exporter — Chrome · Edge · Firefox 115+

One click on the extension and the conversation you're looking at —
ChatGPT or Claude — becomes a single portable, spec-compliant
.curt file on disk. No copy-paste, no cloud, no accounts.

Source on GitHub
Build from source

- 01
One-click export. Open a chat on a supported site, press Export in the popup — the whole thread, in order, lands as one UTF-8 .curt file.

- 02
Spec-compliant by construction. Output is .curt v1 per SPEC.md
docs, and the test suite round-trips every file through curt-format's reference parseCurt.

- 03
Nothing leaves the browser. Zero collection, zero network calls — extraction and serialization happen entirely on your machine. Privacy policy.

- 04
Portable on arrival. The file opens in every app that speaks the format — the viewer, curt-openwith, or anything you build.

Where it works

sitebrowsernotes

chatgpt.comChrome / Edge (MV3), Firefox 115+

claude.aiChrome / Edge (MV3), Firefox 115+

One codebase, two manifests. Chrome and Edge load the MV3 build;
Firefox ships MV3 with strict_min_version: 115.0.

Getting it

The extension is in review for the
Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons (AMO) — store links will appear
here once the listings are live. Until then, build it from source;
it takes about a minute.

Build from source

# requires Node 18+
npm install
npm run build # tsc + Chrome staging -> dist/
node platform/firefox/build.mjs # Firefox staging -> dist/firefox/

Chrome / Edge: open chrome://extensions (or
edge://extensions), enable developer mode, "Load unpacked"
→ dist/.

Firefox: open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox,
"Load Temporary Add-on…" → dist/firefox/manifest.json.

Tests: npx vitest run. Full development notes in the
repo README.

The extension has no backend and makes no network requests. It reads
only the conversation already open in your tab, serializes it locally,
and hands you the file. That's the whole data flow — see the full
privacy policy.

## Launch post — one file, one conversation, kept whole
Source: https://dotcurt.org/posts/2026-10-25-one-file/

The launch post · 2026-10-25 · spec v1 · MIT

.curt — one UTF-8 file, one conversation, everything intact. Images, tool calls, the weird stuff — verbatim.

curt-format@1.2.0 is on npm, MIT. Twenty-seven conformance vectors run in CI so &ldquo;compatible&rdquo; means something.

{
"curt": "curtis-conversation",
"version": 1,
"generator": "your-app@1.2.3",
"extensions": ["images-inline"],
"conversation": { "id": "conv_001", "messages": [ … ] }
}

- 01
The spec — frozen core, v1. New capability never means editing it; it means a registry entry.

- 02
curt-format@1.2.0 — reference implementation on npm. MIT: spec, code, schema, fixtures.

- 03
Twenty-seven conformance vectors — L1 CORE through L4 per-extension — executed in CI. Claiming support is testable.

- 04
Five extensions: images-inline and usage-metadata stable; tool-linkage, agent-context, consensus-receipt draft.

The path is on the adopt page. When you ship, you go in the registry — capabilities.json, public, checkable.

The format is free. The file is yours.

## The preprint — full text
Source: https://dotcurt.org/paper/

.curt

the format
adopt
listen
try
paper
github

Preprint · November 1, 2026 · cs.CY · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23864677 · arXiv pending endorsement

.curt: A Conversations-First, LLM-Native File Format with Executable Conformance for AI Chat Portability

Jordan Newell

Artifact https://dotcurt.org/ · npm install curt-format · MIT · PDF

- conformance27 vectors · passing in CI

- specfrozen · v1

- licenseMIT · permanent

- audit2026-10-14 · public

- implementations11 · public tracker

Abstract

[1, 2]. The 2025–2026 literature has begun to test GDPR rights against generative AI — through compliance surveys of model internals [13], conceptual work on generated data [14], and agentic-AI analyses of the EU Data Act [15] — but no scholarly work treats the conversation archive itself as a portability problem. The one open export specification published outside academia — a nonprofit's conversation-history schema [16] — defines a generic sender/text/channel transcript with no LLM-native semantics, no validation rules, and no conformance testing. We present .curt, a file format and reference implementation filling this gap: a frozen-core JSON envelope — strict whole-file validation, single-file-per-conversation, full-fidelity content including inline binary payloads — extended by a named, additive extension registry, and graded by tiered, machine-executable conformance vectors (L1 CORE through L4 per-extension) run in continuous integration. The specification, reference implementation, JSON Schema, and test vectors are MIT-licensed and published as curt-format on npm. We situate .curt against vendor exports, training corpora formats, agent transport protocols, formal containers (vCon, mbox), and memory-interoperability efforts (PAM, W3C), and we discuss honestly the governance model — a single maintainer with self-reported conformance — and its precedents.

Read alongside

- spec — the normative specification
docs

- vectors — the 27 conformance vectors, plain JSON

- audit — the ecosystem audit, the honest scoreboard

- listen — the listening copy, the paper read aloud

1Introduction

conversations.json in which a conversation is a tree: messages form a directed structure navigated by a “current node” pointer, with each node carrying role, content parts, and recursion metadata. Anthropic's Claude export flattens conversations into message lists joined by parent UUID chaining. Google's Gemini arrives inside a Takeout bundle as activity logs, not conversations at all. Each import path is different enough that every “bridge” tool — the scripts and apps that move conversations between platforms — reimplements parsing from observations of a moving target. None of the exports carry a version. None can be validated: a consumer faced with a malformed file has no rule for detecting it, and typically half-imports whatever parses.

export trap: the data is legally yours and practically unreachable. Portability engineering that starts from vendor exports inherits their instability, because there is nothing stable to target. The market's response is visible and measurable: a micro-industry of bridge tools — browser extensions converting chats across sixteen or more AI sites [18], offline command-line converters, round-up guides — each reimplementing its own parser against an undocumented, unversioned target, and institutional archivists documenting the exports' quirks by hand [17]. Every one of them converts away from the platforms (to PDF, Word, Markdown); none converts between them, because no target schema exists that a second platform could adopt.

conversations-first, LLM-native, and conformance-tested:

- Conversations-first. One file is one conversation. There is no manifest, no account wrapper, no activity log to interpret; a directory of conversations is a directory of files, and bulk transfer is a zip of them.

- LLM-native. The core data model carries what LLM conversations actually contain — roles including tool results, model identifiers, timestamps, and full-fidelity content in which base64 images and tool payloads ride verbatim — with economics and multi-agent provenance available as named extensions rather than bolted-on vendor fields.

- Conformance-tested. A tiered vector suite (27 executable cases) defines what “conforming” means per level, and the reference implementation executes the suite in CI. Claims are graded against vectors, not prose.

curt-format (v1.2.0, the first npm release) with a normative specification, a non-normative JSON Schema, and round-trip fixtures.

Contributions. (1) A problem statement for LLM chat portability grounded in the portability-rights literature, cross-analyzed against the 2025–2026 scholarship: the legal literature has reached generative AI, but the specific slot — conversation archives as a data class requiring an interoperable file format — remains unclaimed. (2) A survey of the adjacent landscape — vendor exports, training formats, agent transports, formal containers, memory-first efforts, and the one open export specification — and of the specific gap each leaves open. (3) The .curt design: frozen core, strict rejection semantics, unknown-field tolerance, extension registry, tiered executable conformance, deterministic bulk naming. (4) An honest account of single-maintainer governance with self-reported conformance, including the precedents that succeeded the same way and the one that did not.

2The right that needs formats

interoperable formats. The recital is the load-bearing one for our purposes: the right is not satisfied by any machine-readable dump, but by data that another system can actually take in.

[1]. Syrmoudis, in the sharpest formulation, shows that the portability right underperforms its competition-and-control goals precisely because “portable” data without actual interoperable formats produces ex situ access to inert files rather than usable migration [2]. The OECD's review of data portability initiatives across services and platforms reaches the same practical conclusion and identifies common formats and interoperability frameworks as the policy lever [3].

[13], analyzes Articles 15, 16, 17, and 22 as applied to data inside model weights — unlearning, explainability, differential privacy — and defines Article 20 in its rights overview without analyzing it; conversation archives, export formats, and interoperability are absent from its 26 pages. Matsumi [14] asks whose data an AI output is, conceptually, without reaching the archive question. Beduschi [15] extends the portability discussion through the EU Data Act for agentic AI acting on the user's behalf — agent-side, not archive-side. The pattern across all three strands: the data class users actually hold — the conversation archive, a class that did not exist when the GDPR was drafted and is now among the most intimate records a person keeps — is never treated as a portability problem requiring an interoperable file format. The slot Article 20 × LLM chat archives is unclaimed, and now demonstrably so: the nearest neighbors are named, and the gap between them is exactly where this paper sits. It does not attempt to fill the slot legally; it fills the precondition the legal analysis identifies: an interoperable format for the data class, published openly, with an executable definition of conformance so that “supports .curt” is a testable claim rather than a marketing one.

published specification that a third party can implement without observing a vendor's behavior; a schema or validation rule set that makes well-formedness decidable, so a receiving controller knows whether it has received what it was told it would; stability guarantees, so a file written today parses after the exporting platform or the importing tool changes; and an executable definition of conformance, so that a controller's claim to accept the format can be tested rather than trusted. No vendor export satisfies any of the four. The design in §4 is .curt's answer, item by item, to this list.

3Landscape

3.1Vendor exports

conversations.json, tree-structured), Claude (message lists with parent-UUID chaining), and Gemini (Takeout activity logs) are discussed in §1. Common properties: undocumented, unversioned, platform-internal, no schema to validate against, no import path on the vendor side. They are the problem statement, not part of the solution space.

3.2Training-corpus formats

conversations array and OpenAI-style and Cohere-style chat JSONL. These are purpose-built for training: role/content pairs, aggressively normalized. They are lossy in exactly the dimensions archives care about: attachments are dropped or referenced externally, tool calls are flattened or elided, model metadata and timestamps are optional at best, and multi-modal content is reduced to text. They also have no validation story beyond “the trainer eventually errors.” Training formats answer “what can a model learn from”; the archive question is “what actually happened,” and the answer needs the fields training throws away.

3.3Agent transport protocols

live inter-agent and agent-tool communication [10, 11]. Persistence is explicitly out of scope for both: a transcript exists for the duration of a session and its canonical serialization is the transport's own event stream, not a durable document. They are complementary rather than competing — an agent framework that speaks MCP still needs a file format for the conversations it produces. A survey of the MCP ecosystem [11] catalogs dozens of client and server implementations and not one durable conversation-archive format among them.

3.4Formal containers

vCon (draft-ietf-vcon-vcon-core-05) is the closest standards-track relative: a JSON container for conversational data, in IETF standardization, with a working group and a dialog data model [4]. Two things distinguish it from what LLM chat archives need. First, its home community is human/real-time communications — voice and video calls, messaging — and its data model has no LLM-native semantics: no assistant/user/system/tool role vocabulary tied to model inference, no tool-call linkage, no model metadata. Its charter explicitly scopes chat logs in, so the fair statement is not that vCon cannot represent chat, but that representing it requires application-private conventions atop a container designed for another domain. Second, conformance: vCon ships no executable test vectors, so implementation claims are checked by reading. We also read vCon's own evolution as evidence for .curt's design bet: the draft deprecates the top-level vcon version field in favor of an extension mechanism — the frozen-core-plus-registry pattern — confirming that containers of this kind are pushed toward additive extension rather than version churn.

mbox (RFC 4155) is the archival precedent worth keeping in view [8]: a decades-old, boring, single-file-per-folder container that outlived every proprietary mail format around it. Its lesson is the container-not-content pattern: the format standardizes envelopes and framing and stays out of content semantics. HAR (HTTP Archive) extends the same pattern to web traffic. .curt adopts the pattern deliberately.

3.5Memory-first efforts

PAM (Portable AI Memory, v1.0) is the most serious peer effort [5]. Credit where due, and specifically: PAM has a named maintainer (Daniel Gines), published governance and semver policy pages, and real technical substance — Ed25519 signatures, W3C Decentralized Identifiers, RFC 8785 JSON canonicalization, and shipped importers for OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI exports. Its gap relative to conversation archiving is orientation: PAM is memory-first. Conversations appear as an index plus companion files in service of a memory graph, not as first-class, self-sufficient single-file archives; and PAM defines no conformance levels, so implementation claims are not testable against vectors. The two projects are, at present, answers to different questions. The memory lane is, moreover, academically active: Ravindran's Portable Agent Memory protocol [19] presents cryptographically verified memory transfer across heterogeneous AI agents, with injection-resistant framing; and Brcic's analysis of AI memory as an infrastructure-layer lock-in problem argues that portability regulation must reach memory graphs [20] — the conversation archive this paper addresses sits directly downstream of that lock-in. That sharpened contrast is itself evidence for the gap this paper fills — the adjacent problem has scholarly work and open protocols; the conversation archive has neither.

W3C AI Agent Memory Interoperability Community Group, chartered in June 2026, confirms institutional interest in the space but has produced no file format [6]. The field is open.

3.6Open export specifications

Data Transfer Initiative (DTI) — a nonprofit devoted to data portability engineering — publishes an “AI Conversation History” schema in a public schema registry (November 2025, revised May 2026) [16]. Its motivation is ours stated by a practitioner body: “Your conversations with your AI tools and services are your personal data,” and its goal is switching AI services “without losing the history, context, and preferences you've built.” The specification itself is a JSON transcript model: conversation-level details (creator, start and end times, modality), an identifiers array of named participant identities, and messages carrying sentAt, sender, text, and channel, with the rule that every sender must appear among the identifiers.

§1, and we distinguish it precisely, because the distinction is the contribution of this paper. The DTI schema is a registry entry: no version number, no stated license on the registry page, no validation semantics, no conformance vectors, no tooling, and a single listed implementation. Its data model is a lowest-common-denominator transcript — a generic sender/text/channel triple with an identity-resolution rule — with no role vocabulary tied to model inference, no tool calls, no model metadata, no attachment story, and no bulk convention. Nothing in it is wrong; it simply answers the transcript-portability question (“who said what to whom, when”) and stops before the LLM-native question (“what did the models do, with which tools, at what cost”). That a portability-focused standards body independently converged on the problem is evidence the problem is real; that its answer stops where .curt's design begins is evidence the design space was open.

4The .curt design

4.1Envelope

.curt file is UTF-8 JSON with a four-field envelope:

{
"curt": "curtis-conversation",
"version": 1,
"generator": "your-app@1.2.3",
"conversation": { }
}

curt is the magic field, matched exactly. version is the format version, matched exactly — the string "1" is a rejection, a rule that costs nothing and eliminates an entire class of lenient-parser bugs. generator is provenance (“writer-name@version”) that readers must ignore: presence, absence, or value never affects parsing, which keeps the format from growing de facto required vendor stamps. conversation carries id, title, createdAt, updatedAt (epoch milliseconds), and messages; each message carries id, role (user, assistant, system, tool), content, timestamp, and an optional model (provider model id, typically on assistant messages). That is the entire core: four envelope fields, five conversation fields, five message fields.

epoch milliseconds for time: no calendar semantics, no timezone ambiguity, trivially comparable, and tolerant at the validator level (version-1 validators accept any JSON number and must not reject fractional or negative values) so that a file written from a language with richer time types is never rejected over its representation. Second, content as a single string: binary payloads ride inline as base64 or data URIs, verbatim. Readers never decode, transform, or re-encode content. This is what “full fidelity” means operationally: the bytes that went in are the bytes that come out, and a small conversation with images may legitimately be a large file. The specification accordingly directs implementers to treat files as untrusted input and bound parsing by size before validation.

4.2Strict whole-file validation

version is exactly the number 1; the conversation and every message carry required fields with exact types. Anything else is a rejection of the whole file — never a best-effort parse that half-imports. The rationale comes directly from the failure mode of vendor exports: when a reader imports “whatever parses,” corruption propagates silently and no one can define what was lost. Whole-file rejection converts silent corruption into a loud, actionable error at a known boundary. The reference implementation's parseCurt returns the parsed conversation or null — null means invalid — and its component predicates (isCurtConversation, isCurtMessage) are exported for reuse, so third-party validators share the canonical behavior rather than re-deriving it.

§4.5) restores the pragmatic middle ground at the level where it belongs — the archive — by requiring readers to import valid entries and report corrupted ones rather than drop them.

4.3Unknown fields: tolerated, preserved where possible

where possible.

[12].

4.4Frozen core + extension registry

extensions array of registry names. Three properties make the mechanism safe:

- Declaration costs nothing. The array is itself an unknown field to old readers: never a validation input, never a reason to reject, whatever its shape.

- Extensions are behaviorally inert at the core. Extension behavior lives entirely in the fields an extension reads and writes inside the conversation and its messages; an extension must not change how the core validates. Malformed extension data cannot corrupt a conforming parse.

- The registry is additive. New entries never change how existing v1 files parse, and entries cannot conflict with core field names. Status moves draft → stable when at least two independent implementations round-trip the entry.

images-inline (stable; payloads inside content), usage-metadata (stable; per-message token counts, cost, provider), tool-linkage (draft; assistant toolCalls linked to tool-role results by toolCallId), and agent-context (draft; multi-agent provenance such as swarm role, leader id, skill ids). Since the first audit, a fifth entry has arrived — consensus-receipt (draft; signed k-of-n consensus decisions bound to the transcript evidence), submitted by the author's own project, tractum — so it exercises the mechanism rather than evidencing adoption: a new capability class entered the format, version stayed 1, and no existing file parsed differently. The core/tool-role split is deliberate: the existence of tool results is core — an LLM conversation without them is not full fidelity — while the linkage schema is still stabilizing and so rides as a draft extension. Cost, token, and provider metadata are similarly placed: widely written, not yet universal, and therefore registry rather than core.

§3.4). .curt starts there: the registry is the only forward-motion mechanism inside version 1, and breaking changes — anything that would make a conforming v1 reader reject or misparse a file it previously accepted — require version 2, never a silent redefinition of 1.

4.5Tiered executable conformance

LevelNameRequirementObligation

L1
CORE
Strict v1 parse/serialize: magic + exact version; whole-file rejection; single leading BOM tolerated; unknown fields preserved where possible on round-trip; any JSON-number timestamps accepted
MUST for “conforming”

L2
NAMED
curtFilename implements the deterministic naming algorithm exactly
SHOULD

L3
BULK
Zip convention; readers never depend on names; corrupted entries reported, valid ones imported
MAY

L4+
per extension
That extension's vectors
MAY

capabilities.json.

§5).

4.6Deterministic naming and bulk transfer

.curt files with no manifest requirement. Entry names SHOULD come from curtFilename, and readers MUST NOT depend on names for parsing or ordering — names are a convenience, never an input. curtFilename is specified so the name depends only on immutable fields: createdAt rendered as a UTC date, a slug derived from the title, and a suffix derived from the id — so the name survives title edits and later updates, orders chronologically, and collides safely. Example: 2025-10-09 fixture-conversation 001.curt.

4.7The Schema artifact

§5). The schema earns its place as an adoption accelerator for tool builders, not as a second norm.

5Governance

One maintainer. dot_curt has a single maintainer acting as BDFL. Spec, registry, and vector changes land as ordinary commits; there is no working group, no chair, no consensus procedure. This is a limitation (§6) and, at the current scale, a feature: the format moves at the speed of its problem, and the audit trail is the git history.

Self-reported conformance. Conformance claims are made by implementers, against public vectors, recorded in a public tracker, with the expectation of a reproducible run. Nothing independently audits the reference implementation either; what makes the system honest is that the vectors are executable and public, so any claim can be checked by anyone in minutes. The first ecosystem audit (2026-10-14) graded the five consumers — all applications within the author's own Curtis ecosystem — and found none passing L1: the reference implementation is the only conforming reader, and the drift concentrates on BOM tolerance and the naming algorithm, precisely the failures the vector suite exists to catch. The tracker exists to make drift visible, and it did.

Precedents. Small-foundation formats have reached ubiquity before, in exactly this shape. JSON was controlled by Douglas Crockford until it was standardized as RFC 8259 [9]; RSS 2.0 was unforked and shepherded by Dave Winer with a frozen spec. The instructive failure is Markdown, whose ambiguity plus single-implementer drift produced the CommonMark fork — a community rebuilding the standard because the original would not move [7]. The lesson .curt takes is to freeze the core early (done: version 1's rules are frozen at release), keep extension as the only motion (done), and donate to a foundation early enough that the fork never becomes the rational move.

Licensing. The licensing story is version-scoped and stated plainly: through release 1.1.0 the spec, reference implementation, schema, and fixtures were BUSL-1.1; as of 1.2.0 (2026-10-14) they are MIT, permanently. A standard that requires permission to implement is not open, whatever its file format is; the MIT relicense was prerequisite to this paper's claims. The Curtis applications that gave rise to the format remain BUSL-1.1 — the moat is in the apps, not the standard.

6Limitations

No cryptographic layer. PAM signs memories (Ed25519) and identifies actors via DIDs; .curt has no signing, no canonicalization, no provenance chain. For conversations — where the integrity threat is corruption, not forgery, and the archive is typically self-produced — we judge the complexity unearned today. The extension mechanism is the migration path: a signatures extension alongside RFC 8785 canonicalization slots in without touching the core, if and when the need materializes.

Preservation where possible. As specified in §4.3, unknown-field preservation is best-effort by design. A pipeline of readers and writers can, in the worst case, shed enrichment fields. Applications that must not lose such fields should treat the .curt file as the system of record and re-read it, rather than relying on intermediate representations.

Container, not content. .curt standardizes the envelope. It does not define content semantics — what a “summary” means, how tool arguments are typed, what a memory is. This is the mbox/HAR/vCon pattern adopted deliberately (§3.4), but it means semantic interoperability between two .curt-reading applications is real only for core fields and registered extensions; everything else is passthrough.

Governance concentration. One maintainer is a bus factor of one, and conformance is self-reported. The JSON and RSS precedents suggest this can work (§5), and the CommonMark precedent suggests what happens when it stops working. The mitigation chosen — frozen core, executable vectors, public tracker — is to make the standard's artifacts independent of any maintainer's continued attention.

Parallel standardization. DTI's conversation-history schema [16] now addresses the same problem statement from the portability-engineering side (§3.6). Two open specifications for AI conversation export could fragment exactly the bridge-tool ecosystem the format is meant to unify. The differences are concrete — LLM-native semantics, validation, conformance — and convergence is a live option in either direction: a .curt interop profile of the DTI identity model, or LLM-native extensions registered against DTI's schema. Competition between open specifications is healthier than competition between proprietary exports, but it is still fragmentation, and it is the landscape's most likely near-term change.

Adoption is unproven. The honest scoreboard: as of the first audit, zero consumers depend on the curt-format package and none of the five consumers is independent of the author; the in-ecosystem implementations — the author's Curtis applications — vendor or hand-roll their parsing, and only the reference implementation passed L1. One consumer has since joined through the registry process — tractum, the author's own project, writer of the consensus-receipt extension — which demonstrates the registry mechanism but is not independent growth: still no independent adoption and no third-party conformance run. The format's technical claims are executable and tested; its ecosystem claims are aspirations with a tracker. The intended sequence — MIT license, then package adoption by consumers, then third-party implementations — has begun to produce evidence: on 2026-11-01 the first package-dependency consumers, the author's own conversion tools (curt-vcon, curt-convert, curt-wildchat), published to npm declaring curt-format as their dependency. This is not independent adoption — every consumer remains the author's — and no third-party conformance run exists; but the tracker records both facts, which is the mechanism working as designed.

7Conclusion and artifact

§6) stands open.

Artifact. The specification (SPEC.md), extension registry (EXTENSIONS.md), conformance vectors (conformance/), ecosystem tracker (capabilities.json), JSON Schema, and zero-dependency reference implementation are MIT-licensed at https://github.com/JordanNewell/dot_curt and published as curt-format@1.2.0 on npm; the spec site is https://dotcurt.org/. Vectors are plain JSON and runnable without the reference implementation; we invite independent implementations and conformance reports.
